summary: A country on the Atlantic coast of southwestern Africa, formerly a Portuguese colony, which went through a 27-year civil war after independence in 1975; oil and diamonds are its main exports.

ranking.name: Catholicism
ranking.description: In 1482 the Portuguese navigator Diogo Cão reached the mouth of the Congo River, and in 1491 the king of Kongo was baptized, so Catholicism entered Angola along with Portuguese colonization. After the Portuguese founded Luanda in 1575, the Catholic Church became closely allied with the colonial government and was the officially supported religion until independence in 1975, which is why it remains the largest denomination today.

ranking.name: Protestantism
ranking.description: From the late 19th century, Protestant missions of British and American Baptists, Methodists and Congregationalists preached in the north, the central highlands and the east, taking root among the Kongo, the Mbundu and the Ovimbundu respectively. The schools these churches ran produced many nationalist leaders; for example, the UNITA leader Savimbi came from a Congregationalist family. After the civil war in the 1990s, Pentecostal and Evangelical churches introduced from Brazil grew rapidly, bringing the Protestant share close to that of the Catholics.

ranking.name: No religion
ranking.description: The MPLA, which governed after independence in 1975, followed a Marxist-Leninist line and at one time restricted church activities, and the long civil war of 1975-2002 also left many people disconnected from the churches. In recent years the young population has grown in cities such as Luanda, and a group of people belonging to no church has appeared, so a little over one tenth of the population identifies as having no religion.

ranking.name: Others (traditional beliefs, etc.)
ranking.description: Traditional beliefs emphasize ancestral spirits and nature spirits, and many Christians still take part in ancestor rituals and healing ceremonies at the same time. Islam was brought mainly by merchants and migrants from West Africa and Lebanon and has very few adherents; Angolan law sets a very high registration threshold for religious groups, and unrecognized groups find it hard to operate legally, so the share of other religions has always remained low.

religion.background: Before the Portuguese arrived in the late 15th century, the peoples of Angola followed ancestral spirits and nature spirits. In 1491 the king of the Kingdom of Kongo was baptized, and Catholicism expanded along with Portuguese colonization and the slave trade, making Luanda a Catholic stronghold of Portuguese Africa. In the 19th century Protestant missions entered the interior, and mission schools became the cradle of the leaders of the three later independence movements (the MPLA, UNITA and the FNLA). The socialist government after independence in 1975 suppressed religion for a time, but after the shift to multiparty politics in the 1990s religious freedom expanded and Evangelical and Pentecostal churches grew rapidly.

ranking.name: Portuguese
ranking.description: Portuguese arrived with the founding of Luanda in 1575 and nearly four hundred years of colonial rule, and at first it was used only by colonists and a small assimilated elite. After independence in 1975, in order to create a common language among dozens of ethnic groups, the government made Portuguese the sole official language and language of instruction; during the civil war large numbers of rural people fled to cities such as Luanda, and the number of native Portuguese speakers rose sharply, so that about 70 percent of the population can now use Portuguese.

ranking.name: Kikongo
ranking.description: Kikongo is the language of the Kongo people of the north, a region that was the core of the Kingdom of Kongo from the 14th to the 19th century, and its capital, Mbanza Kongo, lies within present-day Angola. Because the Kongo people also live in the Republic of the Congo and the Democratic Republic of the Congo, Kikongo is a cross-border language; in Angola it is spoken mainly in Zaire and Uíge provinces.

ranking.name: Kimbundu
ranking.description: Kimbundu is the language of the Mbundu people around Luanda and in the Kwanza River basin; the Kingdom of Ndongo of the 16th and 17th centuries was located here, and Queen Nzinga led her people against the Portuguese. Because the capital, Luanda, lies in the Kimbundu-speaking area, the language has long been strongly influenced by Portuguese, and many young people have switched to speaking Portuguese, so the proportion of speakers has declined.

language.history: Most indigenous languages of Angola belong to the Bantu family, including Umbundu in the south, Kikongo in the north and Kimbundu in the north-central region. From 1575 Portuguese colonization made Portuguese the language of administration and the church, but during the colonial period only a few 'assimilados' could receive a Portuguese education. After independence in 1975 the government used Portuguese as a tool of national unity, and together with the mass urbanization caused by the 1975-2002 civil war, Portuguese quickly became the first language of the majority. In recent years the government has begun trial teaching of indigenous languages in schools to preserve ethnic languages that are gradually disappearing.

ranking.name: Muamba de Galinha
ranking.description: A thick stew of chicken simmered with okra, pumpkin and garlic in red palm oil; it is orange-red in color with a nutty aroma and is usually eaten with funge (cassava paste).
ranking.history: Muamba de galinha is widely recognized as Angola's national dish; 'muamba' refers to the palm sauce made by cooking down the fruit of the oil palm, a traditional crop of the tropical regions of west-central Africa. Okra and pumpkin had already become common in the area in the era of Atlantic trade, and combined with the garlic brought by the Portuguese to give today's flavor. The dish also spread to Brazil and São Tomé, reflecting the exchange of people and food within the Portuguese-speaking world during the slave trade.

ranking.name: Funge
ranking.description: A thick, pasty staple made by continuously stirring cassava flour or cornmeal into hot water; its texture is sticky and smooth and its taste is mild, and it is eaten with all kinds of stews.
ranking.history: Cassava is native to South America and was introduced by the Portuguese along Atlantic routes to the Congo and the Angolan coast in the 16th century; because it tolerates drought and poor soil, it quickly became a staple. In the north and along the coast people mostly eat 'funge de bombó' made from cassava, while the central and southern highlands prefer 'pirão' made from cornmeal. Funge appears at almost every meal, and Angolans consider that without it one has not really eaten.

ranking.name: Calulu
ranking.description: A stew in which dried or fresh fish is slowly cooked in palm oil with sweet potato leaves, okra, tomato and onion; it is salty and savory and often served with funge or rice.
ranking.history: Calulu is most common in Luanda and along the Kwanza River, and the habit of using dried salted fish is related both to local fishing and to the Portuguese culture of salted cod. The name and dish 'Calulu' also appear in São Tomé and Príncipe and in Bahia, Brazil, showing that it crossed the Atlantic with the slave trade. Today it is often served with funge and fried plantain at weekend family meals.

ranking.name: Grilled Fish with Beans (Mufete)
ranking.description: A hearty platter in which a whole fish is charcoal-grilled and eaten with beans stewed in palm oil, fried plantain, cassava and an onion-tomato sauce; it is the representative way of eating on the coast.
ranking.history: Mufete is a representative dish of the Luanda coast, closely connected to the capital's seaside location and its fishing tradition, and the weekend grilled fish at seaside restaurants on the Ilha de Luanda is especially famous. The beans stewed in palm oil (feijão de óleo de palma) combine the local oil palm with beans introduced from the Americas. It is commonly seen at Sunday gatherings of family or friends and is also one of the symbols of urban leisure life after the end of the civil war.

ranking.name: Cocada Amarela
ranking.description: A thick golden dessert cooked from shredded coconut, sugar and egg yolks, sometimes baked to give a fragrant browned surface; its texture is smooth and sweet, with a rich coconut aroma.
ranking.history: Cocada amarela is the product of combining the Portuguese dessert tradition with tropical produce: Portuguese convents were skilled at making sweets with large amounts of egg yolk and sugar, and in the colonial period this technique was carried to Brazil and Angola and combined with the coconuts abundant along the coast. 'Amarela' means yellow, referring to the color given by the egg yolks. It often appears at birthdays, weddings and festivals, and is a dessert commonly seen throughout Portuguese-speaking countries.
